content: Folliculitis refers to the inflammation of one or more hair follicles, and it can develop on any part of the skin. The symptoms of folliculitis typically include the appearance of a rash, itching, and the formation of pimples or pustules near hair follicles. These are most commonly observed in areas such as the neck, groin, or genital region. The pimples may eventually form crusts. The condition begins when hair follicles are damaged. This damage can result from friction caused by clothing, blockage of the follicle, or shaving. Once the follicles are damaged, they often become infected, most commonly with Staphylococcus (staph) bacteria. A specific type of folliculitis known as barber's itch is a staph infection that affects the hair follicles in the beard area, particularly the upper lip. Shaving tends to exacerbate this condition. Another similar condition, tinea barbae, is caused by a fungal infection rather than bacteria. Certain individuals are at higher risk for specific types of folliculitis. For example, pseudofolliculitis barbae is a condition that predominantly affects Black men. This occurs when curly beard hairs are cut too short, causing them to curve back into the skin and trigger inflammation. The diagnosis of folliculitis is primarily clinical, based on the appearance of the affected skin. In some cases, laboratory tests may be performed to identify the specific bacteria or fungus responsible for the infection. It is important to seek medical attention if symptoms recur frequently, persist for more than two to three days, or if the infection begins to spread. Treatment for folliculitis often involves the application of hot, moist compresses to encourage drainage of the affected follicles. Depending on the severity and cause of the infection, treatment may also include topical antibiotics such as mupirocin, oral antibiotics like dicloxacillin, or antifungal medications. Folliculitis generally responds well to treatment, but it has the potential to recur. In some cases, the infection may spread to other areas of the body. These include minimizing friction from clothing, avoiding shaving the affected area when possible, and ensuring that if shaving is necessary, a clean, new razor blade or an electric razor is used each time. It is also important to keep the area clean and avoid using contaminated clothing or washcloths.
